objective: To spell adjectives with the -ous suffix
defs: causing harm or death if swallowed or touched
likely to cause harm or injury
unhappy because someone else has what you want
covered in mountains; very large or hilly
attractive and exciting in a showy way
funny; likely to make people laugh
not to be trusted; secretly dangerous

sentences.poisonous: The brightly coloured frog was ____________________ and the rangers warned visitors not to touch it.
sentences.dangerous: It is ____________________ to cross the road without looking both ways first.
sentences.enormous: An ____________________ wave crashed against the rocks and sent water spraying into the air.
sentences.jealous: She felt ____________________ when her classmate won the art prize she had hoped to win herself.
sentences.mountainous: The ____________________ region was so cold that the highest peaks stayed covered in snow all year.
sentences.glamorous: The ____________________ hotel had a marble entrance and golden chandeliers in every room.
sentences.humorous: The teacher read a ____________________ poem that made the whole class giggle and groan.
sentences.vigorous: The pupils took part in ____________________ exercise on the field, sprinting between the cones.
sentences.thunderous: The crowd gave the winning team a ____________________ cheer as they lifted the trophy.
sentences.treacherous: The mountain path was ____________________ after the rain, so the hikers moved with great care.

starter.question: Can you make these nouns into adjectives using -ous?
starter.ruleBox: Add -ous to a noun to make an adjective. Some bases change: humour → humorous, vigour → vigorous (u dropped).

thisWeeksWordsQ: What do you notice about today's words?
thisWeeksWordsPrompt: Look at the ending of each word. What do they all share?
thisWeeksWordsExplanation: All today's words end in -ous. This suffix turns a noun or root into an adjective meaning 'full of' or 'having that quality'. Some base words change slightly: humour → humorous, vigour → vigorous — the u is dropped.

clicks.label: Original meaning
clicks.body: out of the ordinary; irregular in size

clicks.label: Then
clicks.body: Came into English via Old French enormé in the 1500s.

clicks.label: Now
clicks.body: We use enormous to mean extremely large or massive.

clicks.label: In today's words
clicks.body: The Latin base enormis is hidden inside — the -ous suffix was added to the root in French before entering English.

wordSortQ: Can you sort these words into two groups?

wordSort.box1sub: You can spot a clear English noun inside
wordSort.box2sub: The root changes spelling or has no English base
wordSort.hint: Try removing -ous. Is what is left a real English word?
wordSort.answerNote: Easy to see: dangerous, mountainous, thunderous, poisonous, humorous. Hidden or changed: vigorous, glamorous, treacherous, jealous, enormous.
wordSort.exampleLine: dangerous → danger (clear base) | enormous → enormis (Latin root — hidden)
